p: Bezae and some Latin copies leave out "Philip." Josephus names Herodias' first husband differently.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: τὴν γυναῖκα Φιλίππου τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: the wife of Philip his brother

readings.w: Codex Bezae and some Old Latin manuscripts (as reported by Metzger)

why: The name is in almost every witness and in Mark 6:17. Josephus says Herodias was first married to a half-brother he calls Herod (Antiquities 18.109–110, 136), not to Philip the tetrarch. A few copyists, as Metzger reports, may have dropped the name because of this problem, or to match Luke 3:19, which has no name. See the note on 14:3 for how historians explain the difference.

a: was already many stadia out from land
t: Far from land, or in the middle of the sea?
p: The editions split: NA28 and SBL say "many stadia from land"; Tyndale House and the KJV say "in the middle of the sea."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (03, 300s), the family 13 manuscripts and early Syriac versions (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: σταδίους πολλοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς ἀπεῖχεν
readings.en: was many stadia away from the land
readings.plain: was already many stadia out from land

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (01, 300s), Ephraemi (04, 400s), Washington (W, about 400), the Byzantine majority, Old Latin and Vulgate; Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "in the midst of the sea")
readings.en: was in the middle of the sea
readings.plain: was already out in the middle of the sea

why: Mark 6:47, the parallel, says the boat was "in the middle of the sea," and copyists often made Matthew match Mark. A reading that differs from the parallel is less likely to be a copyist's change, so the NA28 and SBL editors chose "many stadia." The Tyndale House editors weighed the very old support of Sinaiticus and chose the other reading. The meaning hardly changes: either way the disciples were far from shore.
b: A stadion was about 600 feet (185 meters). John 6:19 says they had rowed "twenty-five or thirty stadia," three or four miles.

p: The critical editions say Peter "came" toward Jesus; the Byzantine text says he walked "to go" to him.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Byzantine majority text, Textus Receptus (KJV "to go to Jesus"); Tregelles
readings.plain: so as to go to Jesus

why: The Byzantine wording looks like a smoothing: a copyist may have felt that "he came to Jesus" claimed too much before Peter began to sink. NA28, SBL, THGNT and Westcott-Hort agree on "he came"; Tregelles has "to come." The Greek verb can mean "went toward" without arriving, which is how the Plain English Translation renders it.

p: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus lack "strong"; most manuscripts have it. NA28 prints it in brackets.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (corrected), Ephraemi, Bezae (05, 400s), Washington, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority, Latin and Syriac; NA28 (in brackets), SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "the wind boisterous")
Codex Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03, first hand), 073, 33 and the Coptic versions (as reported by Metzger); Westcott-Hort

why: Nearly all witnesses have "strong," and the adjective could have dropped out by accident. But Sinaiticus and Vaticanus together are weighty, and a copyist might have added the word to explain why Peter feared. The editors kept it with brackets to show the doubt.

p: The KJV's "God commanded, saying" comes from the Byzantine text.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Bezae and others; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Ephraemi (corrected), Washington, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "For God commanded, saying")

why: "Commanded" fits the word "command" in 15:3 so well that a copyist could have brought it in to sharpen the contrast. The plainer "said" has the older support.

t: "His father" or "his father or his mother"?
p: The oldest manuscripts name only the father here. Later ones add "or his mother," as in 15:4–5.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, some Old Latin, the Sinaitic and Curetonian Syriac; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Ephraemi, Washington, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "his father or his mother")
readings.orig: τὸν πατέρα αὐτοῦ ἢ τὴν μητέρα αὐτοῦ

why: Copyists naturally completed the phrase to match "father or mother" just before. No one would have dropped "mother" on purpose. The meaning is the same: the vow frees him from supporting his parents.

t: God's word, God's law, or God's command?
p: Three readings: "word" (oldest), "law" and "command" (Byzantine, KJV "commandment").

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (corrected), Vaticanus, Bezae, Theta, Old Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Ephraemi, family 13
Washington, family 1, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "the commandment of God")

why: "Word" has the widest early support. It also matches Mark 7:13, which could point to harmonizing, but the copyists' habit here ran the other way: "command" repeats 15:3 and is easy to explain as an echo, and "law" is a smaller change of the same kind.

t: "Draws near to me with their mouth"
p: The KJV's longer quotation of Isaiah 29:13 comes from the Byzantine text, which fills in the Septuagint's words.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, families 1 and 13, Latin, Syriac and Coptic versions; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: Ὁ λαὸς οὗτος τοῖς χείλεσίν με τιμᾷ
readings.en: This people honors me with the lips

readings.w: Ephraemi, Washington, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me")
readings.orig: Ἐγγίζει μοι ὁ λαὸς οὗτος τῷ στόματι αὐτῶν καὶ τοῖς χείλεσίν με τιμᾷ
readings.en: This people draws near to me with their mouth and honors me with their lips
readings.plain: This people draws near to me with their mouth, and gives me honor

why: The shorter quotation agrees with Mark 7:6. Copyists who knew Isaiah 29:13 in the Septuagint filled in the missing clause. The added words do not change the point.

t: "Blind guides" or "blind guides of the blind"?
p: Vaticanus and Bezae have only "they are blind guides"; most manuscripts add "of the blind."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Ephraemi, Washington, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority (some in another word order), Textus Receptus (KJV "blind leaders of the blind"); NA28 (in brackets), SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.en: they are blind guides of the blind

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, Bezae (05) and a few others; Westcott-Hort

why: The witnesses that add "of the blind" do not agree on word order, which can be a sign of a later addition. But the phrase also fits the next sentence so well that it may have been lost by a slip of the eye. The editors keep it with brackets.

p: The oldest manuscripts say Magadan, a place no one has found. Later copies changed it to the well-known Magdala.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Bezae, Old Latin and the Sinaitic Syriac; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "Magdala"); some manuscripts "Magdalan"

why: An unknown name is the harder reading. Copyists replaced it with Magdala, the town of Mary Magdalene on the lake's west shore. Mark 8:10 has another unknown name, Dalmanutha, which also caused changes in the manuscripts.

a: When evening comes you say, 'Good weather: the sky is red,'
p: Goes with 16:3. Sinaiticus and Vaticanus lack the weather sayings; NA28 prints them in square brackets, as doubtful.

readings.w: Ephraemi, Bezae, Washington, family 1, the Byzantine majority, Latin, the Peshitta Syriac; SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, NA28 (in square brackets, as doubtful), Westcott-Hort (in double brackets), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: Ὀψίας γενομένης λέγετε· Εὐδία, πυρράζει γὰρ ὁ οὐρανός·
readings.en: When evening comes you say, Fair weather, for the sky is red
readings.plain: When evening comes you say, 'Good weather: the sky is red,'

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, family 13, the Sinaitic and Curetonian Syriac, the Sahidic Coptic, Armenian; Origen; Jerome says most manuscripts in his day lacked them (as reported by Metzger)

why: The case is close. The sayings are missing from strong and early witnesses, and some scholars think they were added from a saying like Luke 12:54–56. Others think copyists in Egypt, where a red morning sky does not bring rain, dropped words that made no sense to them. The SBL and Tyndale House editions print them; NA28 prints them but marks them as doubtful. The Plain English Translation keeps them so the reader can see them, and this note lets the reader remove them.

a: and at dawn, 'Bad weather today: the sky is red and dark.' You can tell what the face of the sky means. The signs of the times, though, you cannot read.
p: Goes with 16:2. Without them, Jesus' answer runs straight from "He replied" to "A generation that is evil."

readings.w: Ephraemi, Bezae, Washington, family 1, the Byzantine majority (which adds "Hypocrites!"), Latin, the Peshitta Syriac; SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, NA28 (in square brackets, as doubtful)
readings.orig: καὶ πρωΐ· Σήμερον χειμών, πυρράζει γὰρ στυγνάζων ὁ οὐρανός. τὸ μὲν πρόσωπον τοῦ οὐρανοῦ γινώσκετε διακρίνειν, τὰ δὲ σημεῖα τῶν καιρῶν οὐ δύνασθε.
readings.en: and in the morning, Stormy today, for the sky is red and overcast. You know how to judge the face of the sky, but the signs of the times you cannot.
readings.plain: and at dawn, 'Bad weather today: the sky is red and dark.' You can tell what the face of the sky means. The signs of the times, though, you cannot read.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, family 13, the Sinaitic and Curetonian Syriac, the Sahidic Coptic; Origen
Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "O ye hypocrites, ye can discern")
readings.en: Hypocrites, you know how to judge the face of the sky
readings.plain: and at dawn, 'Bad weather today: the sky is red and dark.' Hypocrites! You can tell what the face of the sky means. The signs of the times, though, you cannot read.

why: See 16:2: the two verses stand or fall together. The Byzantine text also adds "Hypocrites!", probably from Luke 12:56.

p: The KJV's "the prophet Jonas" follows later manuscripts that copied the words from 12:39.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Bezae, Latin; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Ephraemi, Washington, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "the sign of the prophet Jonas")
readings.en: the sign of Jonah the prophet
readings.plain: the sign of Jonah the prophet

why: The fuller title matches the same saying in 12:39, where all manuscripts have it. Copyists made the two places agree.

t: "You have no loaves" or "you took no loaves"?
p: Here the Plain English Translation follows NA28 and Tyndale House against the SBL edition.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Theta, family 13 (as reported in the NA28 apparatus); NA28, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
Ephraemi, Washington, family 1, the Byzantine majority; SBLGNT, Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV "because ye have brought no bread")

why: The decision rests on the manuscripts: "you have" is read by Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Theta and family 13, the older and more widespread group. "You took" repeats the disciples' own words in 16:7, the kind of echo copyists create. "You have" also matches Mark 8:17, which could itself be a copyist's harmonizing, so that agreement proves nothing either way. The meaning is nearly the same.

a: What are people saying about the Son of Man? Who is he?
t: "Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?"
p: The KJV adds "I": "Whom do men say that I the Son of man am?" The oldest manuscripts lack it.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, some Old Latin and the Vulgate, the Sahidic Coptic; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: Τίνα λέγουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου;
readings.en: Who do people say the Son of Man is?
readings.plain: What are people saying about the Son of Man? Who is he?

readings.w: Bezae, Washington, the Byzantine majority (in different positions), Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: Τίνα με λέγουσιν οἱ ἄνθρωποι εἶναι, τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου;
readings.en: Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?
readings.plain: What are people saying about me, the Son of Man? Who am I?

why: "Me" was probably added from Mark 8:27 and Luke 9:18, where Jesus asks about himself. Because it stands in different places in different manuscripts, it looks like an addition.

p: The KJV's "Jesus the Christ" adds the name; the oldest manuscripts do not have it.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Theta, families 1 and 13, Latin, Syriac; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Sinaiticus (corrected), Ephraemi, Washington, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "Jesus the Christ")

why: The disciples hardly needed to be told his name. The addition reads like a church confession, "Jesus is the Christ," coming into the text.

p: The first hands of Sinaiticus and Vaticanus read "Jesus Christ" here, a rare form in the Gospels.

readings.w: Most manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)
Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (first hands), the Coptic; Westcott-Hort (as reported by Metzger)

why: "Jesus Christ" as a double name appears in Matthew only at 1:1, 1:18 and perhaps here. Some scholars think it marks the turning point of the book (compare 4:17, "From then on Jesus began"). Most editors judge it a copyist's addition, since the two great codices were corrected to the usual reading.

p: The oldest manuscripts have Peter offer to build the booths himself.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi (first hand); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Ephraemi (corrected), Bezae, Washington, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "let us make")

why: "Let us make" matches Mark 9:5 and Luke 9:33. Matthew's "I will make" is the reading that differs from the parallels, so it is more likely to be original.

p: NA28 and SBL say "has been raised"; Tyndale House and the Byzantine text say "has risen."

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus, Bezae; NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
Codex Sinaiticus, Ephraemi, Washington, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority; Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "be risen again")

why: Matthew usually uses the passive "be raised" for the resurrection (16:21; 17:23), while Mark 9:9 has "rise." Copyists may have made Matthew match Mark. Tyndale House weighs the larger and older group of manuscripts for "rise." Either way the point is the same: God raises him, and he rises.

p: The KJV's "Elias truly shall first come" adds "first" from the question in 17:10.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Ephraemi, Washington, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV)

why: "First" repeats the disciples' question and Mark 9:12. The older manuscripts lack it.

t: "Suffers badly" or "is in a bad way"?
p: A small difference between NA28 and SBL on one side and Tyndale House on the other.

readings.w: Ephraemi, Bezae and the later uncials (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "sore vexed")
Codex Vaticanus, L, Z and Origen (Tischendorf); Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

why: "To be badly off" is the ordinary Greek for being sick (4:24; 14:35) and could be original or a copyist's familiar phrase. The NA28 and SBL editors judged "suffers" the less expected word. The sense is the same.

a: Because your faith is so small
p: The KJV's "because of your unbelief" follows later manuscripts. The oldest say "little faith," a favorite word of Matthew.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Theta, families 1 and 13, the Coptic; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.plain: Because your faith is so small

readings.w: Ephraemi, Bezae, Washington, the Byzantine majority, Latin, Syriac; Textus Receptus (KJV "Because of your unbelief")

why: Only Matthew uses the noun "little faith" (oligopistia), and the next words, "faith the size of a mustard seed," need it: the disciples have some faith, but too little. Copyists replaced the rare word with the common "unbelief," perhaps under the influence of "faithless generation" in 17:17.

a: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]
t: "This kind goes out only by prayer and fasting"
p: The KJV's 17:21 is missing from the oldest manuscripts. It seems to have come from Mark 9:29.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (first hand), Vaticanus, Theta, 0281, 33, some Old Latin, the Sinaitic and Curetonian Syriac, the Sahidic Coptic (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.plain: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (corrected), Ephraemi, Bezae, Washington, families 1 and 13, the Byzantine majority, most Latin, the Peshitta Syriac; Tregelles, Textus Receptus (KJV "Howbeit this kind goeth not out but by prayer and fasting")
readings.orig: Τοῦτο δὲ τὸ γένος οὐκ ἐκπορεύεται εἰ μὴ ἐν προσευχῇ καὶ νηστείᾳ.
readings.en: But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.
readings.plain: But this kind does not go out except by prayer and fasting.

why: If the verse were original, no copyist would have a reason to drop it from so many early witnesses in different regions. It is easy to see why it was added: Mark's version of the story ends with Jesus' words about prayer (Mark 9:29), and copyists brought them over. Even in Mark, "and fasting" is itself missing from the oldest manuscripts. The church's practice of fasting before exorcisms and baptisms may have encouraged the addition.
b: Matthew's own answer to the disciples is faith (17:20), not a technique. The added verse shifts the stress to prayer and fasting, which Matthew also values (6:5–18), but in another place.

p: The two Greek words differ by a few letters; the KJV's "while they abode" follows the later one.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, family 1; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
Ephraemi, Bezae, Washington, Theta, family 13, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "while they abode")

why: "Gathering" is the rarer and harder word: it may picture the group regathering in Galilee, or rallying before the road to Jerusalem. Copyists replaced it with the ordinary "staying."

a: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]
t: "The Son of Man came to save what was lost"
p: The KJV's 18:11 is missing from the oldest manuscripts. It appears to come from Luke 19:10.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Theta (first hand), families 1 and 13, 33, the Sinaitic Syriac, the Sahidic Coptic; Origen (as reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.plain: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]

readings.w: Bezae, Washington, the Byzantine majority, most Latin, the Curetonian and Peshitta Syriac; Textus Receptus (KJV "For the Son of man is come to save that which was lost"); some manuscripts add "to seek and" from Luke
readings.orig: Ἦλθεν γὰρ ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου σῶσαι τὸ ἀπολωλός.
readings.en: For the Son of Man came to save what was lost.
readings.plain: For the Son of Man came to save what was lost.

why: The verse is missing from early manuscripts in Egypt, Syria and elsewhere. It matches Luke 19:10 almost word for word, and it makes a smooth bridge from "little ones" (18:10) to the lost sheep (18:12), which is just the kind of link a copyist or a reader in church would add. Its message is true to Matthew (9:13; 15:24), but the words are probably not his.

p: Manuscripts differ on whose Father Jesus names here; the editions follow "your."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Bezae, Washington, family 1, the Byzantine majority; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "your Father")
Codex Vaticanus, Theta, family 13, the Syriac; Westcott-Hort, Tregelles

why: "My Father" may have been copied from 18:10 and 18:19. Both readings are early. "Your Father" turns the parable toward the hearers: God cares for the little ones among you.

p: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus lack "against you." Without it, the rule covers any sin, not only a personal wrong.

readings.w: Bezae, Washington, Theta, family 13, the Byzantine majority, Latin and Syriac; NA28 (in brackets), SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV)
Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, family 1, the Sahidic Coptic; Origen (as reported by Metzger); Westcott-Hort

why: A hard case. "Against you" may have been added from Peter's question in 18:21 ("sinning against me") or from Luke 17:3–4. Or it may have dropped out because the Greek words sound like the ending of the verb before them (hamartēsē eis se). The editors keep it in brackets.
b: The difference matters for church practice. With "against you," 18:15–17 is about settling a personal wrong. Without it, any member who sees a brother sin is to go to him, which makes the passage a general rule of church discipline (see the cards on the chapter page).

p: Tyndale House and the Byzantine text have the slave call his lord "Master"; NA28 and SBL do not.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus and Bezae (Tischendorf); NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles
L and most later uncials (Tischendorf), the Byzantine majority text; Tyndale House GNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "Lord, have patience with me")

why: The fellow slave's plea in 18:29 has no "Master," and Matthew seems to make the two pleas match nearly word for word. A copyist could easily add the natural address. The editions are divided, and the meaning does not change.

p: The Byzantine text adds "at his feet," as the KJV has it.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.en: so his fellow slave fell down

readings.w: Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont), Textus Receptus (KJV "fell down at his feet")
readings.orig: πεσὼν οὖν ὁ σύνδουλος αὐτοῦ εἰς τοὺς πόδας αὐτοῦ
readings.en: so his fellow slave fell down at his feet
readings.plain: threw himself down at his feet

why: The critical editions agree on the shorter text. "At his feet" is a natural detail for a copyist to add. The picture is the same.

a: I will pay it back to you
p: The Textus Receptus adds "all," making the second plea match the first (18:26).

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text (Robinson-Pierpont)
readings.en: and I will pay you back
readings.plain: I will pay it back to you

readings.w: Textus Receptus (KJV "I will pay thee all")
readings.en: and I will pay you back everything
readings.plain: I will pay it all back to you

why: "All" was added from 18:26, where the first slave makes the same plea. In the oldest text the second plea is a little shorter, and a debt of a hundred denarii could really be repaid.

a: forgives his brother from the heart
p: The KJV's "their trespasses" comes from the Byzantine text, perhaps from 6:14–15.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Bezae, Theta, family 1, Latin, Syriac, Coptic; NA28, SBLGNT, Tyndale House GNT
readings.plain: forgives his brother from the heart

readings.w: Ephraemi, Washington, family 13, the Byzantine majority, Textus Receptus (KJV "from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses")
readings.orig: ἀπὸ τῶν καρδιῶν ὑμῶν τὰ παραπτώματα αὐτῶν
readings.plain: forgives his brother his wrongs from the heart
